description:
Cedar Elm (Ulmus crassifolia)

5 July 2016
Ray Roberts Lake State Park, Isle Du Bois
Pilot Point, Denton County, Texas

Cedar Elm is a widespread native tree in the North Texas region. Additional common names for Cedar Elm include Basket Elm, Scrub Elm, Lime Elm, Texas Elm, Olmo, and Southern Rock Elm. The thumbnail sketch for Cedar Elm at the site called Aggie Horticulture states: "Cedar Elm is the most widespread native elm in Texas. It grows in all areas of the eastern half of Texas except the extreme southeastern part. It is a tough, adaptable shade tree with excellent drought tolerance and beautiful golden yellow fall color. Its leaves are small and rough, and glossy green in the spring. Cedar Elm can withstand heavy, poorly drained clay soils and soils that are moderately compacted. It is the only native Texas elm that flowers and sets seed in the fall. Although it is susceptible to Dutch Elm Disease, it appears to be less of a problem with it than it is with American Elm, U. americana, or Winged Elm, U. alata." Cedar Elm grows up to 90 feet high and may take a width of up to 80 feet. The native range for Cedar Elm extends across the eastern half of East and South Texas and on into Mexico's northeast especially northern Tamaulipas and to the north of Texas it extends to Oklahoma, Arkansas, Mississippi, and the southwestern corner of Tennessee. Potentially, it can grow from coast to coast throughout the southern half of the United States, according to the US Forest Service. Its most extensive native range however is endemic to Texas. Because of its North American presence, Cedar Elm is an authentic resident of the Western Hemisphere. Ray Roberts Lake State Park is administered by the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department.

description:
Rough on top, soft on bottom
Piszek Preserve is dominated by eastern black walnuts throughout. Green ash used to co-dominate the canopy in this lowland, but has since mostly declined since the Emerald Ash Borer.

Other common trees here include Acer platanoides, Acer negundo, Ulmus minor, Catalpa spp., Platanus occidentalis, and Ulmus americana.

The understory is dominated by Solidago spp., Artemisia vulgaris, Reynoutria japonica, and Rosa multiflora. Many trees had Celastrus orbiculatus growing on them.

The path was very nice, though. Paved throughout and accessible for bikes and probably for wheel chairs too.

description: Slippery Elm is our most distinctive elm species here in northern Kentucky. Common along the edges of roads and fields, this one is sticking out from the woods along the parking area at NKU's Research & Education Field Station (REFS). Slippery Elm leaves are large and their dense covering of stiff hairs gives them a sandpapery feel. If you give a leaf a hard slap, you can do a leaf magic trick -- it sticks to your hand. (Fair warning: it does this using all its sharp little hairs, so be prepared for some mild itching.) Elm foliage is distinctive even when it won't stick to you. The alternate leaves are two-ranked (sticking out to either side of a twig, but not above or below it) and have double-serrate (big teeth with smaller teeth on them) margins. The leaf bases also tend to be asymmetrical. All in all, easy trees to spot.

The under-surface is smoother in both directions. 
  I now think that  this was not a gift, but a volunteer slippery elm that I accidentally pollarded when it was very young , causing it to send up  several stems from the same base.

description:
Winter tree ID
1- Bark - scale is in inches
2- Twig - slightly hairy, buds of more or less uniform appearance to getting smaller as you go back from the tip, end buds false, branching and leaf scars alternate 
3- Bud scales are two-toned, darker at the edge of each scale
4- Bark not formed in distinct layers 
5- top surface of leaves smooth, but may be hairy beneath 

Compare with slippery elm: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/254731842

Winter tree ID
1- bark - scale is in inches 
2- twigs rough, sandpapery; buds often of two different types, end buds false, branching and leaf scars alternate 
3- buds closest to the tips of the branches dark, pointed
4- buds closest to the trunk may be globular in shape and lighter reddish brown in color.  Examine several branches of more mature trees, as younger trees and not all branches may produce the second type of buds
5- bark is built up in corky, ridged layers
6- top surface of the leaves is rough-hairy, sandpapery 

See American elm for comparison: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/254729925
